title: What am I for?
hookLine: every life is called to love in its own way

lines: A BOY HEARS HIS NAME AT NIGHT.
HE RUNS TO THE WRONG PERSON.
cards: Night, in the temple of the LORD at Shiloh. A boy named Samuel is lying down, and the lamp hasn't gone out yet. He hears his name, gets up, and runs to the old priest, Eli: "Here am I; for thou calledst me."
Eli says he didn't call. Go back to bed. It happens again.
And again. Samuel keeps running to the wrong person. Finally Eli understands, and tells the boy what to say next time.
When the voice comes, Samuel answers: "Speak; for thy servant heareth." Yesterday asked what a human life is for. Today asks it smaller, and closer: what is my life for?

teach.b: Paul's Greek word for calling is klesis.
He writes to the church in Corinth, people who were slaves and free, married and single: "Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called." Calling, and called, side by side.
The ordinary life you're in when the call finds you can be the place where you answer it.

teach.h: NOT ONLY FOR PRIESTS AND MONKS.
teach.b: Martin Luther and other reformers pressed this hard: a calling isn't only for priests, monks and nuns. A farmer, a parent, a shoemaker can each have one.
Catholic teaching speaks of a universal call to holiness, for every baptized person in whatever state of life. Orthodox writers speak of every life as a way toward God.
The churches put it differently; the shared thread is that the call isn't kept for a few. So what is everyone called to?
Paul tells the Galatians: "ye have been called unto liberty," and then what the freedom is for: "by love serve one another." The shape of the call is love.
Your own way of loving is the part that differs: fixing things, listening, teaching, sitting up with a sick parent. And notice Samuel.
He heard the call before he knew who was calling, and kept running to the wrong person.
Some readers find comfort in that: a calling can take more than one try, and sometimes another person, like old Eli, helps you hear it.

how: Christians talk about calling, or vocation, in many settings: some churches pray for people in their daily work, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of callings to marriage, single life, priesthood and religious life.

games.q: you're the boy Samuel. it's night in the house of God, and you hear your name. what do you do?
o: pull the blanket over your head and ignore it.
answer the voice of God straight away.
run to the old priest Eli.
games.why: he runs to Eli: "here am I; for thou calledst me." only after it happens again does Eli teach him to answer, speak; for thy servant heareth.

practice: Skip the job titles, and think of the people in your life and the way you most often end up loving them: fixing, feeding, listening, making them laugh, telling the truth.
Let one line come that starts, I am called to love by, and finish it yourself; if it doesn't come yet, that's all right, Samuel needed more than one call.
If you pray, you can say Samuel's words, speak; for thy servant heareth, and then wait.

wordCard.voice: Calling. Klesis, Paul's word for it. In his letters, a call that finds people in ordinary lives, and whose shape is love.

orig.note: Greek: a calling. Paul's word in abide in the same calling wherein he was called.
